section_summary.extract_value: This section discusses the inverted threshold hypothesis concerning the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement, contrasting it with the traditional threshold hypothesis and a constant relationship. It references several studies, including Park et al. (2007, 2008), Robertson et al. (2010), and Wai et al. (2005), which found intelligence predicted creative accomplishments in highly gifted adolescents. Other studies by Mackinnon (1962), Jauk et al. (2013), Karwowski et al. (2016), and Sligh et al. (2005) are also mentioned, presenting varied support for different threshold models. The section concludes by proposing openness to experience as a critical characteristic for a conditional threshold hypothesis.

section_summary.extract_value: This section explores the 'inverted threshold hypothesis' concerning the relationship between intelligence and creative achievement, contrasting it with the traditional threshold hypothesis and a constant relationship. It reviews several studies, including those by Park et al. (2007, 2008), Robertson et al. (2010), Wai et al. (2005), Mackinnon (1962), Jauk et al. (2013), Karwowski et al. (2016), and Sligh et al. (2005), which offer varying support for these hypotheses. The discussion also proposes that 'openness to experience' may act as a moderator in a conditional threshold hypothesis. Figure 1, adapted from Guilford (1967), illustrates the distribution of divergent productivity scores as a function of IQ, both in its original form and with an overlay showing the intelligence-creativity relationship conditioned on a moderator.
